cues.text: Section two: a Node.js pipeline example.
Let us look at a concrete illustration.
The source gives us an illustrative GitHub Actions workflow, for a repository that contains a lockfile and a test script.
Notice those two assumptions, because the workflow depends on them.
A lockfile records the exact dependency versions, and a test script is the command that runs the project's tests.
Here is the workflow, written in YAML.
I will walk through it line by line, in order.
Please follow along with the visual, because indentation in YAML shows which settings belong to which.
It begins with name, colon, CI.
This simply labels the workflow as "CI", short for continuous integration.
Next comes on, colon, and then in square brackets, push and pull_request.
This is the trigger.
The workflow runs whenever someone pushes code, and whenever a pull request is opened or updated.
That means the checks run early and often, which is the heart of continuous integration.
Then permissions, colon, and indented beneath it, contents, colon, read.
This restricts what the workflow is allowed to do.
It gets read-only access to the repository contents, and nothing more.
This is a least-privilege setting: if something goes wrong in the pipeline, the damage it can do is limited.
Now the jobs section.
We have one job, named test.
Beneath it, runs-on, colon, ubuntu-latest.
This tells GitHub to run the job on a fresh Ubuntu Linux virtual machine.
Then steps, which run in sequence.
Each item begins with a dash.
The first step is uses, colon, actions slash checkout at v4.
This uses a ready-made action that downloads your repository's code onto the runner, so the later steps have something to work on.
The second step is uses, colon, actions slash setup-hyphen-node at v4, with a with block beneath it.
Inside that, node-version is set to the string twenty-two, and cache is set to npm.
So this step installs Node.js version 22, and turns on caching for npm dependencies, which helps later runs go faster.
The third step is run, colon, npm ci.
This installs the project's dependencies.
The source notes that npm ci uses the lockfile and performs a clean install.
In other words, it installs exactly what the lockfile specifies, starting clean, so the result is reproducible rather than drifting from one run to the next.
The fourth and final step is run, colon, npm test.
This executes the project's test script.
If the tests fail, this step fails, and so does the job.
Now let us read the guidance that accompanies the example, because it matters as much as the code.
First, this workflow is a starting point.
You should add lint and security checks appropriate to the project.
Then build an artifact, and stage and deploy it through approved environments.
So the example covers only the test portion; a fuller pipeline continues through build, staging and deployment.
Second, a caution about versions.
The versions shown, such as v4 and Node 22, are illustrative.
They are not claims about the latest versions.
The source adds that production policy can pin action commit SHAs, meaning you reference an action by its exact commit identifier rather than a movable version tag.
Third, a firm rule: a failing step must block promotion.
If any step fails, the change must not move forward toward release.
Fourth, a security warning.
Never deploy untrusted pull request code with privileged production credentials.
Code from an untrusted pull request should never get access to the secrets that can change production.
Finally, the key takeaway.
CI is more than a YAML file.
Writing the workflow does not, by itself, give you continuous integration.
What makes it real is frequent integration of changes, meaningful tests, and fast, useful feedback to the team.
Without those, the file is only decoration.
